title: Cellulitis and Erysipelas: Outpatient versus Intravenous Antibiotic Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult or child with cellulitis or erysipelas: oral versus intravenous antibiotics, hospital referral triggers, antibiotic choice and dose by severity, MRSA cover, reassessment and prophylaxis, using NICE NG141.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG141 does not define severity, give Eron criteria, sepsis tools, inflammatory marker thresholds or outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy criteria; hospital referral criteria are those the guideline states.
Children's vancomycin, teicoplanin and linezolid doses are in NG141 Table 2 but were not read in full; check the British National Formulary for Children.
MRSA agents (vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid) are listed from the extract; confirm with local microbiology.
No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Society of Rheumatology/Infectious Diseases guideline was opened.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: NICE advises an antibiotic for everyone with cellulitis or erysipelas, chosen by severity, site, risk of uncommon pathogens, prior swab results and MRSA status. Oral antibiotics are first choice unless the person cannot take oral medicines or needs intravenous treatment. Intravenous antibiotics should be reviewed by 48 hours with consideration of an oral switch. Infection near the eyes or nose, lymphangitis, suspected uncommon pathogens or spreading infection despite oral antibiotics prompts hospital referral or specialist advice.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and site
actions: Refer to hospital for signs of orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, necrotising fasciitis or sepsis.

Consider hospital referral or specialist advice if severely unwell, infection near the eyes or nose, uncommon pathogens, lymphangitis, spreading infection despite oral antibiotics, or unable to take oral antibiotics.

clinicalManagement.title: Start oral antibiotic
actions: Flucloxacillin first choice for 5 to 7 days; clarithromycin if penicillin allergy; erythromycin in pregnancy; doxycycline is an alternative.
Near eyes or nose: co-amoxiclav for 7 days, or clarithromycin plus metronidazole in penicillin allergy.

clinicalManagement.title: Intravenous antibiotic if needed
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Severe infection or unable to take oral
actions: Flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, cefuroxime, clindamycin or ceftriaxone (ambulatory care only) for 7 days; add MRSA cover (vancomycin, teicoplanin or specialist linezolid) if suspected or confirmed.
Review by 48 hours and switch to oral if possible; consider home or community intravenous antibiotics locally.

clinicalManagement.title: Review
actions: Reassess if worsening or not improving; a course of up to 14 days may be needed after clinical assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Recurrent episodes
actions: Do not routinely offer prophylaxis; specialists may consider a trial for adults with at least 2 separate episodes in 12 months, reviewed at least every 6 months.

regimens.indication: First-choice antibiotic for cellulitis or erysipelas
regimens.dose: 500 mg to 1 g orally; 1 g to 2 g intravenously
regimens.duration: 5 to 7 days (up to 14 days after clinical assessment)
adjustments: No renal or hepatic adjustment is given in the source opened; check product information.
Children: 1 month to 1 year 62.5 to 125 mg; 2 to 9 years 125 to 250 mg; 10 to 17 years 250 to 500 mg four times a day orally; IV 12.5 to 25 mg/kg four times a day (maximum 1 g per dose).
monitoring: Reassess if worsening or no improvement within 2 to 3 days; review IV therapy by 48 hours.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy: use clarithromycin or an alternative.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Able to take oral medicines and does not need intravenous treatment (NICE 1.1.5).
Symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days (NICE 1.1.9).
